lead: Paul arrives in Corinth, a busy port city, and finds a Jewish couple, Aquila and Priscilla, who share his trade. He works with his hands during the week and argues in the synagogue every sabbath. In the Gospel Jesus speaks of “a little while”: the disciples will weep, and then their pain will turn into joy. Psalm 98 sings again that the Lord has made known his victory before the nations.

set: Corinth, refounded as a Roman colony by Julius Caesar, was the capital of the province of Achaia, a crowded trading city between two seas. Paul stayed there a year and six months (18:11). An inscription found at Delphi names Gallio as proconsul of Achaia (see 18:12), and it allows Paul’s stay to be dated to about AD 50–52, one of the firmest dates in his life.

Background. The Roman historian Suetonius writes that Claudius expelled from Rome the Jews who were constantly causing disturbances at the instigation of “Chrestus”. Many scholars think this refers to disputes about Christ within the Jewish community of Rome, and date the expulsion to about AD 49. Aquila and Priscilla may already have been Christians when Paul met them.
str: vv. 1–3: Paul comes to Corinth and works with Aquila and Priscilla.
v. 4: every sabbath in the synagogue.
v. 5: Silas and Timothy arrive; Paul gives himself wholly to the word.
v. 6: opposition, and Paul turns to the Gentiles.
vv. 7–8: the house of Titius Justus; Crispus and many Corinthians believe.
kw: Only here in the New Testament (v. 3). It may mean a worker in leather or in cloth; tents were made of both. Paul was proud to support himself by his own work (1 Thessalonians 2:9; 1 Corinthians 9:15–18).
Reasoned discussion, not shouting (v. 4). The same word describes Paul’s practice at Thessalonica (17:2) and at Athens (17:17).
The leader responsible for the synagogue’s worship (v. 8). Crispus is one of the very few people Paul says he baptised himself (1 Corinthians 1:14).
vv: There he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, who had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla,

Paul later greets them as those who work with him in Christ Jesus and who risked their necks for his life; a church met in their house (Romans 16:3–5). A married couple stands at the heart of the early mission.
he stayed with them, and they worked together
The apostle shares a workshop. The Gospel was spoken over the cutting of leather and the stitching of cloth, as well as in the synagogue.
Every sabbath he would argue in the synagogue and would try to convince Jews and Greeks.
Paul goes first to the synagogue, as always: to Israel belong the covenants and the promises (Romans 9:4). The “Greeks” here are probably Gentiles who worshipped with the synagogue.
“Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.”

Strong words, but they echo the watchman of Ezekiel 33: having given warning, the watchman is not responsible (Ezekiel 33:4–9). They are not a curse on a people. In the next verses the synagogue official Crispus believes, and in the next city Paul again goes first to the synagogue (18:19).
ch: The Second Vatican Council, speaking of the apostolate of lay people, recalls the men and women who helped Paul in spreading the Gospel, among them Aquila and Priscilla (Apostolicam Actuositatem 10, in substance). St John Paul II, in Laborem Exercens (1981), taught that through work a person shares in the activity of the Creator. Paul the tentmaker shows that daily labour and the preaching of the Gospel are not rivals.

r.h: Your pain will turn into joy
set: The Last Supper. Jesus speaks a riddle: “A little while, and you will no longer see me, and again a little while, and you will see me.” The disciples repeat it among themselves, puzzled. Jesus, knowing what they want to ask, answers not with an explanation but with a promise.
str: v. 16: the riddle of “a little while”.
vv. 19–20: weeping now, joy to come.
kw: Seven times in these five verses. The first “little while” leads to the Cross and the tomb; the second to Easter. The Fathers also heard in it the whole time of the Church, short when measured against eternity.
Grief of heart (v. 20). In the next verse Jesus compares it to the pain of a woman in labour, which gives way to the joy of a child born.
Not sorrow replaced by joy from outside, but sorrow itself “turned into” joy (v. 20). The same Cross that caused their tears becomes the source of their joy.
vv: “A little while, and you will no longer see me, and again a little while, and you will see me.”
Within hours they will not see him, for he is arrested, crucified and buried. On the third day they will see him risen.
We do not know what he is talking about.
An honest confession, and the Gospel does not hide it. Not understanding is not the same as not believing.
you will weep and mourn, but the world will rejoice; you will have pain, but your pain will turn into joy.
The disciples’ tears are not wasted. God does not only take sorrow away; he transforms it.
ch: St Augustine, preaching on this Gospel, says that this “little while” is the whole span of the present age: it seems long to us while it lasts, but when it is over we shall see how short it was (in substance). The Church lives in that second little while, between the Ascension and the Lord’s return, with real tears and a joy that no one can take away (16:22).

qa: Did Paul turn his back on his own people at Corinth?

No. He moved next door, to the house of Titius Justus beside the synagogue (v. 7), and the synagogue official himself became a believer (v. 8). Paul’s words are a prophet’s protest that he has done his duty, not a rejection of the Jewish people. He later writes that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1–2), and the Church teaches the same (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 839).
rite: In many countries Thursday 6 May is the Solemnity of the Ascension. In India it is transferred to Sunday 9 May, so today the Easter weekday readings are read. The words “a little while, and you will no longer see me” prepare us well for the Ascension that is near.
study: Paul worked with his hands and preached the word. How can my daily work become part of my witness?
What sorrow in my life am I asking God to turn into joy, and not only to take away?
